reasons: Passages read correctly. ON (Óláfs saga helga, Olaf before Stiklestad): head laid 'i' kné of Finnr, then svefn 'ran a hann' (sleep came over him; the noun is subject, the knee is the goal of a head-laying verb). Hittite KUB 36.89 (Storm-god of Nerik text): the god 'šuppariyanza ēšta' (was sleeping) sweet 'tiešḫuš' in the 'genuwa' of beloved Tešimi. Etymologies are sound: kné = genu- < *ǵónu; svefn < *swep-no-, šupp-/šuppariya- < *sup- (Kloekhorst s.v. šupp-, cognate Skt svap-). But the wording does not match: ON has a noun 'sleep' plus head-laying verb, Hittite a participle plus a different noun (tiešḫa-, not cognate), and the relations differ. 'Sleep in someone's lap' is a near-universal physical description. Both languages would form it with their basic inherited words for knee/lap and sleep, so co-occurrence is expected and carries no phraseological weight. The Hittite text has a Hattic cult setting (Nerik, Tešimi), and the ON scene is a hagiographic pre-battle dream; neither context is comparable in any specific way. The Hittite case ending is an editorial supplement: the tablet has ge-nu-wa, and 〈aš〉 is added by the editor. The knee word itself is transmitted. ON support (Laxdæla 'leggr hǫfuðit í kné henni ok sofnar') shows this is an ordinary ON idiom, not a relic.

reasons: Passages read correctly. bera = φέρω (*bʰer-) and nafn = ὄνομα (*h₁nómn̥) are secure cognates, and RV nā́ma bíbhrat (1.103.4b, 5.30.5b) is the transmitted text, giving a three-branch verb+object pairing. The relation is not congruent across the anchors, however. ON 'bæri tígnar nafn' is a fixed ON social-legal term ('bear a title of rank', e.g. jarl or king), repeated as a stock formula elsewhere in Heimskringla (AM-35-fol 228 has the same 'þeira er eigi bæri tígnar nafn'; cf. 'hafþi ... eigi tígnar nafn', 218). Herodotus 'τὸ οὔνομα τοῦτο ... φέρεσθαι' uses the middle 'carry off / win' (as of a prize, cf. κλέος φέρεσθαι), meaning 'deserve to win the title ὄλβιος'. That is a different construction from Vedic/ON 'bear (carry) a name'. The context similarity (judging a life at its end) belongs to Solon's anecdote and is coincidental to the ON obituary formula. 'Bear a name' is a widely available metaphor (Lat. nomen ferre, Eng. 'bear a name'), so generic risk is real. The Vedic-ON pairing is the defensible core; the Herodotus anchor is the weakest.

reasons: Passages read correctly. ON (Óláfs saga helga, Emundr at Uppsala): 'váro þeir um nóttina' (they stayed [there] for the night). Od. 16.367: 'νύκτ̓ ἄσαμεν' (we spent the night). Both etymologies are sound: nátt = νύξ < *nókʷt-; ON vera/vesa (pret. váru via Verner) < PGmc *wesan- < *h₂wes- (Kroonen s.v. *wesan-1, listing Gk ἰαύω, Skt vasati, OIr. foaid 'spend the night'); ἄεσα < *h₂wes- (Beekes s.v.). Greek ἀέσαι is a genuine collocation: Beekes notes it is 'always with νύκτα(ς)', and with Ved./AV vas- + rātrim it gives a real Greek-Indic pattern (with renewal of the noun in Sanskrit). The ON anchor adds little: vera is the ordinary copula/'be, stay', 'vera (þar) um nóttina / eina nótt' is the routine ON way to say 'stay the night', and the construction differs (prepositional 'um' + definite noun vs bare accusative). Any language with a verb 'be/stay' plus 'night' produces this, so the ON leg is generic. The Greek leg is the valid one, and its distinctiveness rests on the Greek-Indic verb specialisation, not on ON.
